pnpm has been my go-to JS monorepo package manager and script runner for a couple of years. In my view it has almost zero downsides and huge upsides.
pnpm is my default package manager. It is much faster, and disk usage dropped dramatically when I have lots of node_modules in use. Can't recommend it enough.

It works very fast in CI. Its cache is smaller and it builds node_modules much faster. Caching node_modules directly caused side effects and even incidents for us. With pnpm, our install time is 15s vs 35s, which is significant.
pnpm is awesome except when it does not work. That happens very rarely, but it is a nightmare to debug. The rest of the time it is way faster and lighter than npm.

I couldn't use pnpm with an Electron project about two years ago, I think because a spawned process didn't work with symlinks. That's the only time it caused me trouble, and it is much faster than npm.
pnpm doesn't auto-install peer dependencies. That is annoying and forces you to add them to package.json unnecessarily. npm 7+ auto-installs peer deps and is much easier to use in this regard.

I hit glitches with pnpm's scripts that wrap binaries and had to change VS Code launch settings to invoke node directly. Some `pnpx create...` scripts exited the terminal without showing prompts on Windows Terminal. The name is so close to npm that I mistype it, and hitting Ctrl+C has corrupted node_modules a few times. I don't recommend mixing pnpm and npm on a team.

I migrated a large project from yarn to pnpm and the speed difference is insane, both in local development and CI. Some dependencies didn't work properly, but the --shamefully-hoist flag fixed it. Everything works.

We're partway through switching all our monorepos from lerna to pnpm and couldn't be happier. Lerna is slow, cumbersome and can't update deps in subprojects. Everything about pnpm's built-in monorepo support just works: nice, easy and fast.

I'm trying pnpm in a side project and overall I like it. It does feel faster than Yarn 1, but I've found its commands a little fussier to use. If I picked for a new project today, I'd probably go back to Yarn.

In our real-world codebase, pnpm gives around 30% disk savings vs classic node_modules, while Yarn's pnp gives around 80%. pnpm needs compatibility work for packages that wrongly reference transitive or peer dependencies.

We migrated a 20+ package monorepo from Lerna+npm to pnpm and the DX improvement was massive. Install times dropped hugely, and the random errors requiring a full node_modules reinstall are gone. Some production bundles shrank because deps were no longer duplicated. The non-flat node_modules broke imports of undeclared transitive deps, but those were bugs waiting to happen.

We migrated from pnpm to yarn3 with the node_modules linker. pnpm focuses on the wrong things: speed and disk efficiency matter less than the stability, reproducibility and developer experience of yarn3.

I use pnpm only for monorepos, where it works quite well. At times there have been issues with symlinks getting messed up or linking to the wrong dependencies, mainly when multiple versions of the same package are involved.
pnpm seems the lightest of the bunch, but why mess with symlinks and confuse other tools? I'm possibly just salty that Metro doesn't support symlinks; otherwise I'd be on the pnpm love-train.

I moved a workspace from yarn classic to pnpm and noticed the difference at first install. The non-flat layout means packages can't use deps not listed in their package.json, which gives a clean dependency tree. Recursive/parallel commands replaced my need for Lerna. Installs across multiple projects are fast because packages are already on disk.
Why must minimumReleaseAge go in a workspace file, which you may not have outside a monorepo, rather than package.json? Anyway, it's progress.
Am I the only one who hates the decision to no longer support corepack? Corepack was fine and there is already too much churn. Another commenter: it dampens my enthusiasm for pnpm v12 a bit.
I migrated a Node 24 repo to pnpm 12 and it works absolutely fine with corepack out of the box.

Several users complained the pnpm 12 release post reads as LLM-written and is hard to parse. One example quoted: 'a specifier now names a repository rather than choosing a transport.' One said: 'Time to hop off I guess. They don't even bother to write changelog on their own.'
